text:
Chapter 25: The Curtain

The secret garden bloomed and bloomed, and every morning revealed new miracles. In the robin’s nest there were eggs, and the robin’s mate sat upon them, keeping them warm with her soft, feathery breast and careful wings. At first she was very nervous, and the robin himself watched over her with fierce protectiveness. Even Dickon did not go near their quiet corner in those days. Instead, he waited until, through the silent working of some mysterious spell, he had reassured the little birds. He made them feel that everything in the garden was just like them, and that everyone understood the wonder of what was happening—the immense, tender, overwhelming, and heartbreaking beauty of those eggs. If even one person in that garden had not known in their very soul that taking or hurting an egg would make the whole world spin out of control and crash through space to its end—if anyone had failed to feel this and act accordingly—there could have been no happiness in that golden spring air. But they all knew it and felt it, and the robin and his mate knew that they understood.

At first, the robin watched Mary and Colin with sharp anxiety. For some mysterious reason, he knew he didn't need to watch Dickon. The very first moment he set his bright, dew-like black eye on Dickon, he knew he was not a stranger. He was just a kind of robin without a beak or feathers. Dickon could speak the robin language, which is distinct and unmistakable. To speak robin to a robin is like speaking French to a Frenchman. Dickon always spoke it to the bird, so the strange gibberish he used with humans didn't matter at all. The robin assumed he spoke this gibberish to them because they weren't smart enough to understand feathered speech. Dickon's movements were also very robin-like. He never startled anyone with sudden, threatening gestures. Any robin could understand Dickon, so his presence was not disturbing in the least.

But at first, it seemed necessary to be on guard against the other two. To begin with, the boy creature did not enter the garden on his own two legs. He was pushed in on a wheeled contraption, covered in the skins of wild animals. That by itself was suspicious. Then, when he began to stand up and move around, he did it in a strange, awkward way, and the others had to help him. The robin used to hide in a bush and watch this anxiously, tilting his head from side to side. He worried that the slow movements meant the boy was preparing to pounce, the way cats do. When cats are getting ready to spring, they creep over the ground very slowly. The robin talked this over with his mate for a few days, but then he decided to drop the subject. Her terror was so great that he feared it might harm the eggs.

When the boy began to walk by himself and even move more quickly, it was an immense relief. But for a long time—or at least it felt long to the robin—he remained a source of anxiety. He did not behave like other humans. He seemed very fond of walking, but he had a habit of sitting or lying down for a while, and then suddenly getting up in a startling way to start walking again.

One day, the robin remembered that when his parents taught him to fly, he had done almost the same thing. He had taken short flights of a few yards and then had to rest. So, it occurred to him that this boy was learning to fly—or rather, to walk. He mentioned this to his mate. When he told her that their own eggs would probably do the same thing once they grew feathers, she was completely comforted. She even became eagerly interested and enjoyed watching the boy over the edge of her nest, though she was sure her own eggs would be much smarter and learn faster. Still, she remarked indulgently that humans were always clumsier and slower than eggs, and most of them never seemed to learn to fly at all. After all, you never met them in the air or on the treetops.

After a while, the boy began to move around just like the others, but all three children still did unusual things at times. They would stand under the trees and move their arms, legs, and heads in a way that was neither walking, running, nor sitting down. They practiced these movements every day at regular intervals. The robin could never explain to his mate what they were doing or trying to do. He could only say he was sure their eggs would never flap about like that. However, since the boy who spoke fluent robin was doing it too, they could be sure it was not dangerous. Of course, neither the robin nor his mate had ever heard of the champion wrestler, Bob Haworth, or his exercises for building muscle. Robins are not like human beings; their muscles are exercised from the very beginning, so they develop naturally. When you have to fly around to find every single meal, your muscles never waste away from lack of use.

Once the boy was walking, running, digging, and weeding like the others, a great peace and contentment settled over the nest in the corner. Fears for the eggs became a thing of the past. Knowing the eggs were as safe as if they were locked in a bank vault, combined with having so many interesting things to watch, made sitting on the nest a highly entertaining job. On rainy days, the mother bird actually felt a little bored because the children did not come into the garden.

But even on rainy days, Mary and Colin were far from bored. One morning, as the rain poured down without stopping, Colin was starting to feel a bit restless. He had to stay on his sofa because it wasn't safe for him to walk around the house yet. That was when Mary had a brilliant idea.
“Now that I am a real boy,”
Colin said,

“my arms, legs, and my whole body are so full of Magic that I can’t keep still. They want to be active all the time. Mary, do you know that when I wake up in the morning, when it’s early and the birds are singing loudly outside—and everything seems to be shouting for joy, even the trees and things we can’t actually hear—I feel like I have to jump out of bed and shout too! If I did that, just think of what would happen!”
Mary giggled uncontrollably.
“The nurse and Mrs. Medlock would come running,”
she said.
“They’d be sure you had lost your mind, and they’d send for the doctor immediately.”
Colin laughed too. He could picture exactly how they would look—how horrified they would be by his sudden outburst, and how amazed to see him standing on his own two feet.
“I wish my father would come home,”
he said.

“I want to tell him myself. I think about it all the time. We can’t keep this up much longer anyway. I can’t stand lying still and pretending anymore, and besides, I look completely different now. I wish it weren’t raining today.”
That was when Mary had her inspiration.
“Colin,”
she began mysteriously,
“do you know how many rooms there are in this house?”
“About a thousand, I suppose,”
he answered.
“There are about a hundred rooms that no one ever enters,”
Mary said.

“And one rainy day, I went and explored a lot of them. No one ever found out, though Mrs. Medlock almost caught me. I lost my way on my way back and stopped at the end of your corridor. That was the second time I heard you crying.”
Colin sat up quickly on his sofa.
“A hundred rooms no one goes into,”
he said.
“That sounds almost like a secret garden. Let's go and look at them! Wheel me in my chair, and nobody will know we're gone.”
“That’s exactly what I was thinking,”
Mary said.

“No one would dare to follow us. There are long galleries where you could run, and we can do our exercises there. There is a little Indian room with a cabinet full of ivory elephants, and all sorts of other rooms.”
“Ring the bell,”

Colin said.

When the nurse came in, he gave his orders.
“I want my wheelchair,”
he said.
“Miss Mary and I are going to look at the unused part of the house. John can push me as far as the picture gallery, since there are stairs. After that, he must leave us alone until I send for him.”

Rainy days lost all their gloom that morning. Once the footman had wheeled the chair into the picture gallery and left them alone as ordered, Colin and Mary looked at each other with delight. As soon as Mary made sure that John was safely back downstairs, Colin got out of his chair.
“I am going to run from one end of the gallery to the other,”
he said,
“and then I’m going to jump, and then we will do Bob Haworth’s exercises!”
They did all of those things, and many more. They looked at the portraits and found the plain little girl dressed in green brocade, holding the parrot on her finger.
“All these people must be my relatives,”
Colin said.

“They lived a long time ago. The one with the parrot is, I think, one of my great-great-great-great-aunts. She looks a bit like you, Mary—not as you look now, but how you looked when you first arrived. You are much healthier and better-looking now.”
“So are you,”

Mary replied, and they both laughed.

They went to the Indian room and played with the ivory elephants. They found the rose-colored brocade sitting room and the hole in the cushion that the mouse had made, but the mice had grown up and run away, leaving the hole empty. They explored more rooms and made far more discoveries than Mary had on her first journey. They found new corridors, hidden corners, flights of stairs, old paintings they liked, and strange antique objects they didn't know how to use. It was a wonderful, entertaining morning. The feeling of wandering through the same house as everyone else, yet feeling miles away from them, was absolutely fascinating.
“I’m glad we came,”
Colin said.
“I never knew I lived in such a huge, strange old place. I like it. We’ll explore it every rainy day. We’ll always find new, interesting corners and objects.”

All that activity gave them such a good appetite that when they returned to Colin’s room, they didn't leave a single bite of their lunch untouched.

When the nurse carried the tray back downstairs, she set it down on the kitchen counter with a thump, making sure Mrs. Loomis, the cook, could see the clean, empty plates.
“Look at that!”
she said.
“This house is full of mysteries, and those two children are the biggest mysteries of all.”
“If they keep eating like that every day,”
said John, the strong young footman,
“it’s no wonder he weighs twice as much as he did a month ago. Before long, I’ll have to quit my job for fear of throwing my back out.”

That afternoon, Mary noticed something different in Colin’s room. She had spotted it the day before but hadn't said anything, thinking it might have happened by accident. She didn't speak now either, but sat looking intently at the portrait over the fireplace. She could see it clearly because the curtain had been drawn back. That was the change she noticed.
“I know what you want me to tell you,”
Colin said, after she had stared for a few minutes.
“I always know when you want to ask me something. You’re wondering why the curtain is drawn back. I’m going to keep it that way.”
“Why?”
Mary asked.

“Because it doesn’t make me angry to see her laughing anymore. Two nights ago, I woke up in the bright moonlight. I felt as if the Magic was filling the room and making everything so beautiful that I couldn’t stay in bed. I got up and looked out the window. The room was quite bright, and a patch of moonlight fell right on the curtain. Somehow, that made me go over and pull the cord. She looked right down at me, and she seemed to be laughing because she was glad I was standing there. Now, I like looking at her. I want to see her laughing like that all the time. I think she must have been a magical person.”
“You look so much like her now,”
Mary said,
“that sometimes I think you are her ghost turned into a boy.”
That idea seemed to strike Colin. He thought it over, then answered slowly.
“If I were her ghost, my father would love me,”
he said.
“Do you want him to love you?”
Mary asked.
“I used to hate that he didn't care for me. If he grew fond of me, I think I would tell him about the Magic. It might make him happier.”
